h1: Fencing in Plano, TX: Installation, Repair and Gates
heroSub: Plano caps rear fences at 8 feet, wants front-yard fences under 40 inches and half open, and most subdivisions add an HOA on top. Call now and compare two or three written quotes from independent fence contractors.
introHtml:
Fencing in Plano usually starts with one of three problems: a gray, leaning wood fence that has outlived its pickets, a section that came down in a spring storm, or a driveway gate that stopped opening. Many Plano subdivisions date from the 1980s to the 2000s, so a lot of backyards are on their second or third fence, and a lot of lots are alley-loaded with a gate or two to deal with.

White Rock Fence Co is advertising for independent fence contractors. It does not build, repair or install anything itself. Call (214) 555-0137 and your request goes to an independent fence contractor who quotes the job in writing, and we suggest you get two or three comparable quotes before you pick one.

services.title: Wood privacy fence installation
services.desc: Replacing a worn 6-foot fence or stepping up to board-on-board with cedar pickets and steel posts. One DFW firm advertises installed cedar privacy fence at $18 to $28 per linear foot; another advertises $30 to $60 for 6-foot wood, so prices vary widely.

services.title: Fence repair after storms and age
services.desc: Leaning posts, missing pickets and wind-damaged sections. Plano's city handout says a permit is not required for repairs to an existing fence that do not exceed 25% of its area in a 12-month period.

services.title: Gate repair and automatic gates
services.desc: Sagging walk gates, worn hinges, dead openers and sliding tracks. Power wiring for an opener is electrical work, so ask the installer who holds the electrical license.

services.title: Wrought iron and ornamental fences
services.desc: Iron or steel pickets for a front yard, where Plano wants fences under 40 inches and at least 50% open. One Dallas-area firm advertises residential tubular steel at $30 to $45 per linear foot installed.

sections.heading: What the City of Plano says about fences
sections.html:
Plano's Residential Fence Permit handout, from the city's Building Inspection Department, is short and worth reading before you sign a contract. It says a fence may not exceed 8 feet, and that a front-yard fence may not exceed 40 inches and must be at least 50% open. A site plan goes in with the permit application, and a final inspection is required.

The same handout says masonry fences, brick columns and retaining walls over 4 feet need a Texas-registered engineer, and that corner lots must keep sight visibility clips. Plywood, corrugated steel, barbed wire and fiberglass panels are on the prohibited list. The handout sends you to the fee schedule for the permit cost, so ask the City for the current number instead of trusting a figure from a website.

Plano's handout does not say whether fence contractors must register with the city, unlike Dallas, Richardson and Irving. Ask the City, and ask any contractor for proof of insurance. Texas does not license fence contractors at the state level, so never take a claim of being licensed at face value. For prices and the wider picture, see the fence cost guide and fence installation pages, and confirm every rule with the City and your HOA.

sections.heading: HOAs, alleys and shared fences in Plano
sections.html:
Many Plano neighborhoods sit under an HOA. Under Texas Property Code Sec. 202.023, an association generally cannot stop you from installing a perimeter fence as a security measure, but it can still regulate the type of fencing. In practice that means getting written approval of the style, height and stain color before the contractor orders a single picket.

On alley-loaded lots and corner lots, ask the contractor how the City's sight-clip rule applies to your corner, because a solid fence and a gate swing near the alley or street can run into it. Texas811 says Texas law requires you or your contractor to call 811 two business days before digging, and that if you hire a contractor it is the contractor's responsibility. Ask who is making that call.

If the fence sits on the boundary and both neighbors use it, Texas Law Help says both neighbors own it and share the cost of repairing and replacing it. That is general information, not legal advice. Talk to the neighbor before the quotes arrive, not after.

sections.heading: Repair or replace: comparing Plano quotes
sections.html:
A fence that is 15 to 20 years old and leaning usually raises the same question: is another round of repairs worth it? For scale, one Dallas-area firm advertises single post replacement at $150 to $400 and leaning section straightening at $300 to $800 per section, while another DFW firm advertises storm damage repair at $300 to $1,200. For a full replacement, that second firm advertises $3,000 to $4,500 installed for 150 linear feet of cedar. Much of the Dallas area sits on expansive clay that swells and shrinks with moisture, which is one reason posts shift, so ask each contractor how they set theirs. See fence repair for more.

For board-on-board, firms disagree on the premium. One DFW firm says it adds $2 to $5 per linear foot over a basic dog-ear fence, and another says about 30%. We could not find a published Dallas-area price for an 8-foot fence, so ask for 6-foot and 8-foot figures on separate lines of the quote. These are one firm's advertised numbers, not this site's quote.

When you compare quotes, make them match: same footage, height, picket material, post material, number of gates, haul-away of the old fence, and who handles the permit paperwork. Gate trouble is its own line, so see gate repair and iron fences if that is your job.

faq.q: How tall can a fence be in Plano, TX?
faq.a: The City of Plano's fence permit handout says the maximum height is 8 feet, and a front-yard fence may not exceed 40 inches and must be at least 50% open. Your HOA can be stricter than the city. Confirm both before you order materials.

faq.q: Do I need a permit to replace a fence in Plano?
faq.a: The city's handout describes a permit application with a site plan and a final inspection, and says a permit is not required for repairs to an existing fence that do not exceed 25% of its area in a 12-month period. Whether your full replacement counts as new work is a question for Plano's Building Inspection Department, so call before the crew starts.

faq.q: Does a Plano fence contractor need a license?
faq.a: Texas does not license fence contractors at the state level. Some cities register contractors, including Dallas, Richardson and Irving, but Plano's handout does not say either way. Ask the City whether registration applies, and ask any contractor for proof of insurance.

faq.q: How much does a fence cost in Plano?
faq.a: This site does not quote prices. One DFW firm advertises installed cedar privacy fence at $18 to $28 per linear foot, another advertises $30 to $60 for 6-foot wood, and Ergeon's Dallas County page lists wood at $38 to $48 per foot. They disagree, so get two or three written quotes with the same specs.
